Below is a complete empirical research plan tailored to your setting and data.

1. Identification Strategy
Primary strategy: Triple-differences (DDD) difference-in-differences

- Rationale: Eligibility requires simultaneously being at least age 50 and residing in one of the eligible districts, and the policy begins only in the program period. This yields three clean margins—time (pre vs program window), geography (eligible vs ineligible districts), and age (50–53 vs 46–49 at inflow)—that allow a saturated DDD to difference out (i) time shocks common to all, (ii) region-specific shocks affecting all ages, and (iii) age-specific shocks common across regions. To tighten comparability across space, we implement the DDD locally around the border using the constructed travel-time distance to the boundary.
- Complementary robustness: Difference-in-discontinuities (DiDisc) in age at 50. We estimate the jump in unemployment duration at age 50 in eligible districts during the program and subtract the corresponding age-50 jump in (a) the pre-period and/or (b) ineligible districts. This absorbs any intrinsic discontinuity at 50 unrelated to REBP (e.g., tenure rules, norms).
- Treatment intensity IV: Instrument actual/potential UI entitlement (weeks) with the predicted eligibility indicator (Post × EligibleDistrict × Age50plus) to estimate the effect per additional week of potential UI on unemployment duration (LATE), accommodating imperfect measurement of the 780-week work-history condition or imperfect take-up.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable:
  - Intent-to-treat (ITT): REBP eligibility at unemployment entry: Treated = 1 if (Post window) × (resides ≥6 months in an eligible district) × (age ≥ 50 at inflow) × (meets 780-week prior employment). In practice, we will:
    - Directly compute the 780-week condition from ASSD where possible; if incomplete pre-1972 coverage prevents certainty, we use the provided continuous employment and experience-ratio ≥ 0.7 filter and, as robustness, run a fuzzy design via IV using predicted eligibility as instrument for potential UI weeks.
  - Treatment timing/event date: Unemployment spell start date. Pre: 1986-01-01 to 1987-12-31. Program: 1989-08-01 to 1991-07-31. Exclude mid-1988 to mid-1989 to avoid confounding from announcement/rollout.
- Control group (counterfactual):
  - All other cells entering the DDD: (i) age-ineligible 46–49 in eligible districts, (ii) age-eligible 50–53 in ineligible districts, and (iii) pre-period entrants. Identification comes from the triple interaction; the model uses all eight group-time-age cells.
  - Spatially local controls: Restrict to communities within a symmetric travel-time bandwidth (e.g., ≤45 minutes) around the eligible-ineligible border to ensure similar labor markets.
- Running variable and cutoff (for the DiDisc robustness only):
  - Running variable: age in days/weeks at inflow; cutoff at 50 years.
  - For a spatial DiDisc, we additionally use travel-time distance to the border with cutoff at 0, implementing results within a narrow spatial bandwidth.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- A1: DDD parallel trends. In the absence of REBP, any changes over time in unemployment duration for older vs younger workers would be the same in eligible and ineligible districts. Plausibility: Reasonable given otherwise uniform labor market institutions across Austria and the local-border design. The DDD absorbs region×time and age×time shocks; remaining concern is region×age×time shocks tied to steel restructuring disproportionately affecting older workers—addressed via near-border restriction and pre-trend checks.
- A2: No manipulation of assignment around thresholds.
  - Age cannot be manipulated.
  - Residency must be established ≥6 months pre-spell; moving to gain eligibility is possible but costly. We will test for differential pre-spell mobility near the border by age and period, and use longer pre-residency windows (e.g., ≥12 months) as robustness.
  - The 780-week condition is predetermined; we restrict to long continuous work histories. Plausible.
- A3: No cross-border spillovers affecting the control. Labor demand or employer behavior in ineligible districts near the border should not be meaningfully altered by REBP in eligible districts. Plausibility improves with narrow border bandwidths; we will check for spillovers using placebo outcomes and inflow rates.
- A4: Stable composition of inflows across cells, or selection that is differenced out by DDD. We will verify pre-period balance and run selection diagnostics (inflow counts, covariate distributions).
- A5: SUTVA and stable policy implementation. REBP rules are national and sharply defined; implementation is uniform.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigations
- T1: Selective migration to eligible districts to gain access at 50.
  - Mitigations: (i) Require ≥12 months pre-residency as robustness; (ii) document mobility rates by age relative to the border before/after; (iii) donut around the border (exclude communities within, say, 5 minutes of the border where strategic moves might concentrate); (iv) show results on individuals with long-term residence (e.g., ≥3 years).
- T2: Differential shocks from steel restructuring hitting older workers harder in eligible districts (region×age×time confound).
  - Mitigations: (i) Border-local sample; (ii) rich controls (district trends, employer-industry FE of pre-separation firm, pre-spell wage/tenure); (iii) pre-trend/event-study graphs for 1986–87 vs 1988; (iv) DiDisc in age that nets out any intrinsic age-50 discontinuity by comparing eligible vs ineligible or pre vs program.
- T3: Fuzzy treatment due to imperfect measurement of 780-week eligibility or incomplete take-up.
  - Mitigations: (i) Construct likely-eligible sample directly from ASSD work histories when feasible; (ii) report ITT (policy effect of eligibility) and IV estimates using Post×Eligible×Age50 as instrument for predicted potential UI weeks; (iii) show strong first stage.
- T4: Endogenous entry into unemployment (e.g., older workers or firms engineer separations post-policy).
  - Mitigations: (i) Focus on inflows and condition on pre-separation employer and industry FE; (ii) restrict to separations flagged as mass layoffs or firm closures; (iii) reweight post-period covariates to match pre; (iv) show that inflow rates by age at the border evolve smoothly except for treated cell.

5. R Code Outline
Assumptions:
- CSVs: assd.csv (employment histories, employer region/industry, demographics), aur.csv (unemployment spells with start/end, community of residence, socio-econ), regions.csv (district_id, eligible_district, community_id, dist_to_border_min).
- Variable names assumed and constructed below; adjust as needed.

Packages
- fixest for high-dimensional FE DID
- data.table for efficient data handling
- lubridate for dates
- sandwich/lmtest for robust inference
- AER or fixest for IV
- ggplot2 for diagnostics

R code:

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(AER)       # for ivreg if needed
library(ggplot2)

# 1) Load data
assd <- fread("assd.csv")   # columns assumed: id, dob, sex, emp_start, emp_end, employer_id, employer_industry2d, district_id_emp
aur  <- fread("aur.csv")    # columns assumed: id, unemp_start_date, unemp_end_date, unemp_duration_weeks, residence_community_id, pre_sep_employer_id
regions <- fread("regions.csv")  # columns: community_id, district_id, eligible_district, dist_to_border_min

# 2) Prepare spell-level data
# Merge residence info
setnames(regions, c("community_id"), c("residence_community_id"))
aur <- merge(aur, regions, by = "residence_community_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Dates and windows
aur[, unemp_start_date := as.Date(unemp_start_date)]
aur[, unemp_end_date   := as.Date(unemp_end_date)]

# Compute age at inflow
assd[, dob := as.Date(dob)]
aur <- merge(aur, unique(assd[, .(id, dob, sex)]), by="id", all.x=TRUE)
aur[, age_years := as.numeric(floor((unemp_start_date - dob) / 365.25))]

# Windows
aur[, pre := unemp_start_date >= as.Date("1986-01-01") & unemp_start_date <= as.Date("1987-12-31")]
aur[, post := unemp_start_date >= as.Date("1989-08-01") & unemp_start_date <= as.Date("1991-07-31")]
aur <- aur[pre == TRUE | post == TRUE]

# Sample restrictions
# Ages 46-53
aur <- aur[age_years >= 46 & age_years <= 53]

# Non-steel-sector inflows: use pre-separation employer industry from ASSD
# Build mapping from employer_id to industry2d using most recent pre-sep record
emp_ind <- unique(assd[, .(employer_id, employer_industry2d)])
setnames(emp_ind, "employer_id", "pre_sep_employer_id")
aur <- merge(aur, emp_ind, by="pre_sep_employer_id", all.x=TRUE)

# Define steel indicator if needed; here assume "27" or similar; adjust to actual coding
aur[, steel := (employer_industry2d %in% c(27L, 28L))]
aur <- aur[steel == FALSE | is.na(steel)]

# Work-history filters: continuous histories and experience ratio >= 0.7
# Construct prior work weeks in 25 years pre-inflow (if observable)
# Approximation: compute total weeks employed in [unemp_start_date - 25y, unemp_start_date)
assd[, emp_start := as.Date(emp_start)]
assd[, emp_end   := as.Date(emp_end)]
setkey(assd, id)

get_workweeks <- function(id, start_date){
  window_start <- start_date - years(25)
  # pull person's employment spells
  sp <- assd[J(id=id), .(emp_start, emp_end)]
  if (nrow(sp) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  # intersect with window
  sp[, start_int := pmax(emp_start, window_start)]
  sp[, end_int   := pmin(emp_end, start_date)]
  sp <- sp[start_int < end_int]
  sum(as.numeric(end_int - start_int))/7
}

# Compute for each spell (can be heavy; for production, pre-compute)
aur[, weeks_worked_25y := mapply(get_workweeks, id, unemp_start_date)]
# Potential weeks in 25 years
aur[, weeks_potential_25y := 25*52.18]
aur[, exp_ratio := weeks_worked_25y / weeks_potential_25y]
aur <- aur[exp_ratio >= 0.7 | is.na(exp_ratio)]  # keep flexible if missing

# Likely meets 780 weeks (=15 years)
aur[, likely780 := weeks_worked_25y >= 780 | (exp_ratio >= 0.7 & !is.na(exp_ratio))]

# Residency duration filter (if available). Suppose aur has 'months_resided_pre' variable.
# If not, skip or approximate from registry moves; here we assume availability:
if ("months_resided_pre" %in% names(aur)) {
  aur <- aur[months_resided_pre >= 6]
}

# 3) Key treatment indicators
aur[, age50plus := as.integer(age_years >= 50)]
aur[, elig_dist := as.integer(eligible_district == 1)]
aur[, post_ind  := as.integer(post)]
aur[, pre_ind   := as.integer(pre)]

# Spatial bandwidth around the border: 45 min baseline
aur <- aur[!is.na(dist_to_border_min)]
aur[, absdist := abs(dist_to_border_min)]
sample_bw <- 45
aur_local <- aur[absdist <= sample_bw]

# Month-year FE of inflow
aur_local[, ym := format(unemp_start_date, "%Y-%m")]

# Dependent variables
# Primary: registered unemployment duration in weeks (provided)
# Robustness: time to next job if available; assume aur has time_to_next_job_weeks

# 4) Main DDD specification (by sex; also pooled with sex interactions)
# Treated triple interaction
aur_local[, DDD := post_ind * elig_dist * age50plus]

# Controls: smooth functions of age and distance; FE for district and month
# Create age in months for flexibility
aur_local[, age_months := round((unemp_start_date - dob)/30.44)]

# Baseline DDD pooled, with rich FE and slopes
# Cluster by district_id
est_main <- feols(
  unemp_duration_weeks ~ DDD +
    post_ind:elig_dist + post_ind:age50plus + elig_dist:age50plus +  # all two-way interactions
    poly(age_months, 2) + poly(dist_to_border_min, 2) +
    i(sex) +                                                # sex FE
    i(pre_sep_employer_id) +                                # pre-sep employer FE (optional; may be many)
    i(employer_industry2d)                                  # industry FE
  | district_id + ym,                                       # district and month-year FE
  cluster = ~ district_id,
  data = aur_local
)

summary(est_main)

# Heterogeneity by sex: interact DDD with female
aur_local[, female := as.integer(sex %in% c("F","Female"))]
est_sex <- feols(
  unemp_duration_weeks ~ DDD*female +
    post_ind:elig_dist + post_ind:age50plus + elig_dist:age50plus +
    poly(age_months, 2) + poly(dist_to_border_min, 2) +
    i(pre_sep_employer_id) + i(employer_industry2d)
  | district_id + ym,
  cluster = ~ district_id,
  data = aur_local
)
summary(est_sex)

# 5) Robustness check A: Narrower spatial bandwidth (20 min)
aur_local_20 <- aur[absdist <= 20]
est_bw20 <- feols(
  unemp_duration_weeks ~ DDD +
    post_ind:elig_dist + post_ind:age50plus + elig_dist:age50plus +
    poly(age_months, 2) + poly(dist_to_border_min, 2)
  | district_id + ym,
  cluster = ~ district_id,
  data = aur_local_20
)
summary(est_bw20)

# 6) Robustness check B: Treatment intensity IV (LATE per week of potential UI)
# Construct potential UI weeks under policy rules
aur_local[, pot_ui_weeks := ifelse(post_ind==1 & elig_dist==1 & age50plus==1 & likely780==1, 209, 30)]
# First stage: strong effect of DDD on pot_ui_weeks expected
fs <- feols(pot_ui_weeks ~ DDD + post_ind:elig_dist + post_ind:age50plus + elig_dist:age50plus +
              poly(age_months, 2) + poly(dist_to_border_min, 2)
            | district_id + ym,
            cluster = ~ district_id, data = aur_local)
summary(fs)

# 2SLS with fixest iv
est_iv <- feols(
  unemp_duration_weeks ~ 1 | pot_ui_weeks ~ DDD + post_ind:elig_dist + post_ind:age50plus + elig_dist:age50plus,
  vcov = ~ district_id,
  data = aur_local
)
summary(est_iv)

# 7) Event-study style diagnostic on pre-trends (placebo with 46–49 only)
# No effect expected for 46–49 across eligible vs ineligible over time
placebo <- feols(
  unemp_duration_weeks ~ post_ind*elig_dist +
    poly(age_months, 2) + poly(dist_to_border_min, 2)
  | district_id + ym,
  cluster = ~ district_id,
  data = aur_local[age50plus==0]
)
summary(placebo)

# 8) Optional: Plot means by cell for transparency
cell_means <- aur_local[, .(mean_dur = mean(unemp_duration_weeks, na.rm=TRUE)),
                        by=.(post_ind, elig_dist, age50plus, female)]
print(cell_means)
```

Notes:
- High-dimensional employer FE may be heavy; drop if memory-bound.
- Cluster at district level; as robustness, cluster by district×period or use Conley-type standard errors if spatial correlation is a concern.

6. Expected Results
- Direction: Positive. Extending potential UI from 30 to 209 weeks should reduce exit hazards and lengthen registered unemployment spells via liquidity and moral-hazard channels.
- Magnitude: Because most spells end well before 30 weeks, the average ITT effect among 50–53 is likely modest but non-trivial. A back-of-the-envelope based on prior UI elasticity evidence suggests roughly 0.2–0.4 week increase per 1-week increase in potential benefits is too large for this age group and context; more realistic is 0.05–0.10 weeks per potential-week at the mean, implying 10–20 weeks for a 179-week increase if it fully binds for a subset. Hence, an average increase of 6–15 weeks for men and 10–25 weeks for women seems plausible, with larger effects for women due to the ability to bridge to early retirement at 54–55. The IV estimate (per week of potential UI) should be small (0.03–0.08), reflecting that only a fraction reach the new cap.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
- C1: Parallel trends for DDD (pre-period) verified with diagnostics: 1 if pre-trends flat near the border for 46–49 vs 50–53; otherwise 0.
- C2: No manipulation at thresholds (age, residency, work history): 0.5–1. Age is clean (1); residency could be selective (0.5); work history mostly predetermined (0.75). Overall: 0.75.
- C3: No spillovers across the border: 0.75. Local labor markets may interact; restricting to narrow bandwidth and placebos improves plausibility.
- C4: Strong first stage/sharp treatment definition: 1. Eligibility rules are sharp; first stage on potential UI weeks should be very strong.
- C5: Correct specification and inference: 1. Rich FE, flexible controls in age and distance, clustering at district; plus robustness (bandwidths, IV, DiDisc placebos).

Overall, the DDD around the border with strong robustness (DiDisc at age 50 and IV for treatment intensity) should credibly identify the causal effect of the large extension of UI on unemployment duration, and how it differs by gender given early retirement rules.
